proposed_features.description: Age ranges correlate with income potential; younger individuals may be early in career, while older individuals may have accumulated wealth or be retired.
Higher education levels are associated with higher income potential due to access to professional roles.
Certain occupations (e.g., professional specialties) are associated with higher income compared to manual or service roles.
Marital status may influence income through dual-earner households or financial responsibilities; married individuals may have higher combined income.
Presence of capital gains suggests investment activity or asset appreciation, which is more common in higher-income individuals.
The size of capital gains can indicate wealth accumulation, with larger gains associated with higher income groups.
Self-employment or private sector roles may offer higher income potential compared to government or other sectors.
Higher weekly hours may correlate with higher income, especially in hourly or labor-intensive jobs.
Numerical education level (education-num) provides a direct proxy for education attainment, which correlates with income.
Relationship status (e.g., husband, not-in-family) may indicate household structure and financial responsibility, affecting income level.
Historical and systemic factors may influence income distribution across racial groups, making this a relevant feature.
Gender may correlate with income due to occupational segregation or wage gaps, even when controlling for other factors.
